I like to take my girl to the bathing sea
Cherished by Lawrence Dilley Summer breaks the love of love
I bet you don't remember old man Sweeney
I don't remember who I remember I got a new memory too. You remember him? Yeah.
Maybe we have to turn that fan off. We won't have that off long. Put this thing on here.
No, you don't answer. Just attach that. That's all right.
Is that all right on there? I'm going to put a little cloth or something on there first. I don't think it won't rattle or anything. I think it'll be okay, though. I'll put the telephone.
You better turn it off for a second.
Mutt Cherry died up there, too. Yes, he died in 1948, I think, September of 1948. Sam was pretty good there.
I knew Mutt very well. Wonderful trumpet playing. His style of playing.
Mutt. I wanted to ask you a few questions about your life. I was from Hornville.
Yeah.

He was born right in the city. Weren't the Carey's, I think? Or were they from the country? No, he was born in Hornville. Oh, he was up there? Hornville, Louisiana. Oh, up there. We were up there for a parade.
Parade just about two weeks ago. Hornsville.
Now, where were you born, Mr. Dewey? I was born in the Playa Rue, 1887. What's the exact...
April 30th.
April 30th. Yeah. And when did you go to New Orleans?

When you're alone, you have to answer all the time. Oh, yeah, that's right. I remember, 1901 when Jack Dawson lied on to just work up in 91. But I wasn't involved in long before then, but I can't remember what year it was.
Long before 1901. What was your first instrument? What did you start to play? My first instrument was a guitar. A guitar.

We had a brother's band in Laplace. My mother was a singer, my grandmother was a dancer. My daddy was a violin player. My older brother trombone player. The doctor played bass violin, guitar, and I had a cousin playing. We had a brother the whole day's band in Laplace. So the clan that played a dad and I, that made me put the clan at home. We began to run up the scale. The first thing you know I was playing the tune. And playing since.
Now who did you play with in New Orleans first then?
First, now I played with Piron on the roof garden.
That big and high building is still there, isn't it? No, that's down. Oh, I thought the one by the city hall.
Used to be the first, no, that's the first precinct where the first precinct used to be.
The Pythian Temple or something, isn't it?
Yeah. That's down.
And that's down? Yeah.
Well, then I've been looking at the wrong building.
Yeah, the wrong building.

That's across the street from the Paris Preal. No, no, no. Put the picture in the wrong building. Yeah, that's the first place I played with Piron. But I came to Norway, we came to Norway with Kid Ory from Laplace. But we disbanded because Kid and Ory were getting to get too big and big, so his head began to swell. We wanted the orchestra a piece. So he got, he got his orchestra, I got one too. I was playing with Frank at Ducey. Oh, the Eagle Band. The Eagle Band. Yes. Buck Johnson was playing. Yeah, Buck, me, Buck, Eagle Band. Yeah. And I remember you went to Fuclos. I went to Fuclos, 101 Ranch. We had the train at Harry Wills. Yeah. Yeah. Oh, yeah. 101 Ranch. That's right. I can, Arnold Duferche and that, that tell them from across the river. Lala, the one the managing Harry Wills. Yeah. And I played at that time with Piron. I played tranchina, Roosevelt Gold Room, Farbacher, Antoine, those are the white places I mentioned. Where? Southern Yard Club. Southern Yard Club. Southern Yard Club. The Italian Hall. In fact, that's how I called it. Then no talking about color. He was all the way. Talking about color there.
Spanish Hall. Oh, yeah.
When we had that Spanish, we had that discussion on Sunday there. They'd take that old train and we bucked. About 20 bands out there on that beach on that lake. Good old days. Good old days.

Yeah. Well, when they played at Antoine's, did they have music regularly or just for a certain party? Nightly. Nightly. Every night? Piron played there nightly. Piron played there nightly. Right in the main dining room. Yes, ma'am.
Gee, I never knew they had music. You all played on the JS Sydney a while too, didn't you?
No. The captain. I didn't go with Sydney a Vene, but Sydney a Vene left me was playing with me at the Hunt.
No, I mean, they both leave that Canal Street going to Resilient.
No. Uh-uh. I made one trip. Oh.
I mean, there was a hide there.

I remember Piron, I saw that job. Piron, yeah. Red Sydney, you remember Sydney? Yeah, yeah. We used to laugh at Sydney. He used to cut off. He used to cut off. Remember we used to laugh at him? Yeah, I remember.
Any other bands in New Orleans that you played with that you can remember?
Well, I played with Tigg Chambers. Who else? Who else was Tigg Chambers? You know. Who else was in Tigg Chambers band? How did they spell that name? Is it Tick or Tigg?
T-I-G. T-I-G. T-I-G. T-I-G. T-I-G. T-I-G. T-I-G. T-I-G. T-I-G. T-I-G. T-I-G. T-I-G. T-I-G. T-I-G. T-I-G. T-I-G.
T-I-G. T-I-G. T-I-G. T-I-G. T-I-G. T-I-G. T-I-G. T-I-G.
T-I-G. T-I-G.
T-I-G. T-I-G. T-I-G. T-I-G. T-I-G. T-I-G. T-I-G. T-I-G. T-I-G. T-I-G. T-I-G. T-I-G. T-I-G. and he's the first to bring it out there. We used to go listening.
What style did he play? Something like Louie or Bunk?
Something more like Bunk Johnson.

He had a big tone, most people say. Oh, it was a much more powerful man, but that style. That style, mm-hmm. When you went to Chicago, what was that date that tells here on this contract? That's April 1917. That's correct. Who all was in that band?
Sugar Johnny, Louie Kepard on the guitar, Roy Palmer, Herbert Lindsay, Eddie Garland, and Toby Hall on the drums.
Then we added Lil Hardin.
How was it? The Deluxe?
Deluxe, and switching to Deluxe of Drinks.
That's what they left New Orleans with, that's what I'm calling it. Yeah, that's that first contract. Yeah, and Deluxe, he had me on the bass. Yeah, that's the Deluxe. Roy Palmer. Yeah, yeah, Deluxe.
Deluxe office, yeah. This contract says something here, I believe, about Thomas Smith. Is that his real name? Johnny Smith. Johnny Smith.

That's that bro here, when bro was with me. Yeah, I've seen the scratch. I've never seen the original though. That's the original thing. But that Lil's face is scratch on there, but that's where he wrote it. Yeah, Lil's face got... Yeah, broke, took over Eddie Garland.
Tells here they paid, what was it, 85 or $80 to each member then of the band. Nice picture. That's a nice old contract.
What do they call themselves, the New Orleans Jazz Band, Bill, isn't that in the first part?
That's right, that's why there's a book in that book there, New Orleans.
Yeah, the contract here says the New Orleans Jazz Band.

That must have been number two, but they had two orchestras left, but the Dixalan, you remember, bro, used to put that livery stable blue? Yeah, the rocker. Yeah, the rocker and shield. Yeah. Yeah, the ritual. They're still written in there. They had a colored man, Manuel Perez, all that was up there for them. These men, is it Mitchell Lacalze, C-A-L-Z-I?

That's the booker. He was the booker, and this Lee Krauss. Krauss, that's two partners. Two partners. They're the ones that booked you. That's correct. Into the deluxe. That's right. Yeah, that's so nice. We saw Louis Capard, have you seen him lately?
No, I've seen him something like that. I haven't seen him in 1919.
He's over in the city all the time. I'm going to go to see him pretty soon.
I was there for Cap Jones, you know, and I didn't know that. I thought he was dating.
Well, Louis Capard, he moved. He used to be on Roman Street. That's where I knew him from here, Roman. He's on, he moved. I'll send you his address next time. I sure will. I appreciate it.
Next time you get over, you can go to see him. But you can avoid that, because I'm going there pretty soon. I can use the phone, true Willie Humphrey. Yeah, yeah.
I had dinner with a woman for his son of the rest.
Yeah, Willie Humphrey, he'd chair me all around there. We're not teaching that band here. I wanted to see the old man. I went to see the old man too, stroke. I didn't know the old man had a stroke.
Yeah.
You always used the Albert system.
Always did. Yeah, always did.
Can you tell us about the old style clarinet players? The first ones you heard, different style. Who were some of the better players that you heard?
Well, we had Willie Warner. Yeah. And Frank Gwynn. That old one. Zed. Zed. Kaiser. Kaiser. Kaiser.
I heard Fess talk about Zed a lot. Yeah. And Manuel Mineta.
Did you ever play with Manuel Mineta? Oh, yeah. We played in Storerville, one or two years.
I told him yesterday we were coming up to see you and he said to say hello to you.
Yeah, Manuel and Peter Bucow and all that bunch from across the river there.
Walter Nixon.
Yeah. Walter Brundy.
Yeah, Walter Brundy.
I wondered about the early clarinetists. Did they sometimes play more of the lead or did they always play that part of the chorus?
I'm going to tell you, at that time, big ol' Louis was the clarinet man in New Orleans. Yeah, it was tops. He played the lead because he used the C clarinet, played the violin part.
Him and George. Yeah.

And Teal. George Mackey. George Mackey. But George Mackey. Lawrence and Teal. Yeah, they played B and A clarinet, but Louis used only C, played the violin, played the violin part. Yeah. He played the lead sheet all the time.
And who was the first one to start to play that other style of, you know, the chords and the arpeggio?

Well, it was like that mostly, mostly start two or three mostly start together because we all used to go listening and everyone had the different ideas in playing the fingering and the execution, you see. This guy played one way, he'd make a diminished scale, the other played another way, make straight scale and also, so that you can't hardly tell because most of all, there's no hardly trying to play in New Orleans, play the light.
Play the light notes.
Every one of different styles.
Different styles. Different styles.
Different styles. That's right.
Now that chorus to high society, you know, that they all played, do you know who started that? Was that a piccolo part or something?
Piku Composer. You think Piku Composer? Yeah. He's a clarinet player downtown.
Yes, I know Piku.
Well, I went to his place too the other day. He wrote, he comported it.

He was playing with Mr. Brower, you know. That's right, yeah. He plays a clarinet right now, man. He's a clarinet. Still can play all right. Maybe not quite like he used to, but he still gets around all right.
No, he do play well. Yeah.
No color, yeah. I don't do like I used to, but I let them know what I'm playing. Yeah, that's true. Yeah. Well, I want to play.
I see you have a plastic reed. Do you think they work all right?

Yes, sir. You know, those are the old ten-cent reeds. We used to have them go two for a quarter, three for a quarter. Sometimes they get thick up in your shirt, and then you wouldn't have no reed to play, see? Yeah. And you have to get the nickel and put two nickels together to get it even, see? And get a cigarette, imagine light it up, it's quite even.
I've seen people do that. Do you like the Albert system better? Did you ever try the Bain system? I tried.
I couldn't do no business with him. I couldn't do no business.
Do you think this has a better tone than the other one?
No, the tone is that, it's not the instrument. The tone is in the lip.
It's in the lip.
Comes from the artist. Yeah.
Do you have any advice for a young kid that would be starting clarinet? Would you advise him to take up the Albert system, or?

Well, I would advise them how to use the reed, the pressure on the reed. What would they do to get a good tone? Well, you see, they get a good tone, I find it. It's simple. Sure. Now, the fellow that uses his teeth, he don't have good pressure like the one that don't.
Yeah.
You know what I mean? Cover your lip over it. Yeah, you see your teeth, kills that tonation, the teeth. Yeah. But by not having none, well, your tones come in.
In other words, you have better lip control when you use the lip.

Yeah. Well, you know, you need some repair. Some players, I know, put their upper teeth down there, and others, I think Barney Bigard uses what they call the French embouchure, putting both lips. Yeah, I think so, yeah. Oh, you advise that, putting both lips together?
Yeah, because you can, you can, if you have the slur, you can make that, what they call the lip slur. Lip slur. If you use the teeth.

Now, Bessier, he used that because he used to make a whole lot of things, he'd make you make an immediate chicken or something, you see. Well, he, and some other things he used to make. Comes from the lip. From the lips. Mm-hmm.

That's using his lips. Very controlling the lip. Well, somebody told me once, I believe Wilbur Swetman used to have an act, he'd play two clarinets at once, and then Sidney, he'd take his clarinet and he'd take one piece off at a time, you know, the bell. I used to do that, too. Yeah, and finally end up with the mouthpiece. Yeah, I used to do that, too. How long did you stay in Chicago with that band?
How long I stayed in Chicago? I was then the race ride. I was then. Oh, the 1919 race ride. Oh, yeah, I was then.
You left there around 1921, or?

Some really, about 23, I think. Yeah. Oh, I was going to ask, I always wondered, you know, I mentioned to Mr. Bro the other day, too, when I was talking to him about when you had two clarinets in the band, you and Sidney, you played the lead, or did one play the lead?

Always played the lead, and Sidney was the hot man. He was the hot man. Always the hot man. Always was Peter. And you played more of the straight melody. Straight to let them know what's coming on, because he never could read, see, at that time. Yeah. But the minute you played it once over, that's all he tells you, let me have it. A whole lot of it he takes, too, I'm talking about. Oh, he's a great clarinetist. Oh, yeah.
Well, he's the best in the business for second, man. I'm telling you.
I'm telling you. He's hard to do.
The freezing and the coloring. It's like I'm showing you with a couple. Natural ability.

Yeah, it can't be the I'm showing you with a couple. I don't care where you're coming from. Well, we were talking about Louie a minute ago. Where do you think he got his style? From Oliver or from Bunk? When did you play with Bunk? You say first in the Eagle Band a little bit way back? Then we went to Noir and Lyrie. Can you tell me about that Banner Band, because I don't know much about that. Well, there's a cut in there. So that picture, just a minute, let me see if I can find that. And you can mention who's in that. Oh, yeah, sure. Because Bunk doesn't even look natural to me.
He's a young Bunk. I don't know if you keep him from drinking. That one was in the Banner Band. I don't know if you keep Bunk from drinking.

And who is the trombone player? The trombone, that's Gus Fortnay. Oh, I met him then, sure. Sure. At Bunk's funeral, he was there. Yeah, sure. And I stopped later on the way home. And he played at the town down a little bit farther. I met Gus, yeah. I forgot his last name. Gus Fortnay. And that's Bunk. And then who's the? Evan Thomas. And the drummer? Robert Stafford. Stafford. Drummer. You say he's in California now?
No, no idea.

Oh, he's still in New Iberia. Or the piano. He's in Los Angeles. William Boyner. Burnham? B-R-N-E-R. Burner. Yeah. Burner. Oh, I knew something like that. Burner played sax. A friend of Dink Johnson. Did you ever know Bill Johnson and Dink Johnson? I know Dink. I know Dink Johnson. He's dead now, too. That's Ed Reedom. He's dead. The banjo is Ed Reedom.
R-E-D-O-M. Reedom. Uh-huh.
And the tenor sax. Tenor sax.
That's Tom Edwards.
Tom Edwards.
And this is you. That's me. And the album? That's Classe Roy. Classe Roy. Played in third sax. Third sax.
Classe Roy. Roy. R-O-Y. R-O-Y. And who's the bass player? John Sandis. John Sandis. That was a big band. One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten.

New Orleans couldn't come in in New Iberia then. You really like that band? Oh yeah, we killed New Orleans. I mean, we killed till it's there. Don't come in New Iberia, not there when we was there. Now, don't Bunk always want to play with you again? The last few years. Bill Bucking, that last album, he came right here. Two or three times. Flood Rain. You know, you know, the old one can play those numbers on the one. He named him. All the more, the only one. The old Redback Bucking. Oh, he had one. I'm sorry. I'm sorry. I'm sorry. I'm sorry I didn't go. I could have gone. Yeah, I wish you had made some. George wouldn't have had that break. Well, I give George a break. George has got a break. You see, everything happens for the best.
Yes, sir. Sometimes, well, either way, you've been here and been happy.
Yeah, I've had mine, so I'll let the other fellas have a chance.
George has been traveling around lately, but he's not so well. I guess the road hasn't agreed very well with him either. So it's tough to be on the road. On the road, yeah.
Unless you know how to take care of yourself. You've got to be like this guy and I, see if we know the road question. It requires a meal to rest. I'm telling you. Meals and rest. I don't get it.
In the Banner Band, what part did Bunk play? I may be asking a lot of questions about Bunk, but he was a very close friend of mine and I admired him so much. I'm just interested in.

He played the second something under E.T. Thomas, because he knew how that second part would go with his tone. Did you all use music in the Banner Band? Oh, yes. Everybody was reading. Everything was reading. Oh, yeah. Everybody read that.
Did you play all the popular tunes? Did you play many?

All, all, we even played the, that, the Dall Dance. That was a difficult number for playing a piano player. I always had a piano player, but we knocked that off. The Dall Dance. That was a . Full of trippets. Yeah, that was a difficult piano. We knocked that out of the Banner Band. Did you play the old rags, too? Oh, yeah, old rags. We played Banner Band, played everything but over the shoe.
And when was that Banner Band about? When were you with it and when was Bunk with it?
Well, I was, I was there until the 27th. I don't know how that's done when the flood, the flood ran us up in Texas. And the flood took water. I stayed there about eight years, I can remember.
When do you think, how long you started there in 1921 or so maybe then? I guess so around the 20s, yeah. When was Bunk in it then, when you joined?

Not when I first joined, but after I was in there, well, I got him. You don't know just 20 joined then? No, I don't know when. I used to go to New Orleans and get substitutes, you know, with plays, just like I did in the Black Eagle. Black Eagle, I went and got Earl Humphrey and John Joseph, Irvin Joseph on drum. Irvin, that's my cousin. Yeah, Tom Benton.
Oh, he had banjo or guitarist. Yeah, well, I got reinforced those country bands. I was bunking the Black Eagle band too for a while. Yeah, uh-huh. With you, same time as you? No, not same time.
Later, I guess. Mox was in the same time. Mox, another homeboy. Yeah. Yeah, sack of mute.
T-Boy was playing with that band once too. Where's T-Boy? T-Boy Rene? You know, you remember Johnny French, bro?
Johnny Frank? Yeah.
No, I know.

Oh, yeah, you know Johnny French. You remember Johnny French and Marshall, one where his trumpet plays? Oh, yes, yes, I do. Johnny French appreciates banjo, he's got a big choice. That's a good rap. Oh, well.
Who were the best trumpet players you ever heard, would you say? I've never heard no one, no better than E.T. Thomas.
Really? For high, high workout. For high register. He was, he was, well, how strong, you know what he is.
Yeah.

High C's. Somebody said he was trained up in Boston or so. No, sir, he was trained under Professor O'Jay right in Crowley. Oh, right in Crowley. Yeah, the man there, Professor O'Jay, had five years conservatory playing in all foreign countries. He played from a bazoon up. And you'd whistle a tune and you'd have a white shirt and you'd write the lead sheet, and about an hour he'd have an arrangement for a six-piece band, and how great he was.
Did you hear Freddie Kepard too? I guess you... I had Freddie Kepard. And that was my favorite.

I had Freddie Kepard and King Oliver in the same job. How did they all compare? They didn't get long, because Freddie always wanted more money than Joe. Freddie thought he could get better. Well, he got it. Yeah, he did, because he, I don't want no use, but I want $50 a week. He called him King Kepard.
Well, what does that story, he said, how the reason you and Bishay broke up, the reason he left the band?

Oh, Bishay won't save prices as the manager, that's the trouble. Yeah. Because he read and I read and he didn't read. He won't save prices. I told you, you don't get it. He said, well, I don't stay. Well, he goes there, Joe, you'll grab him right off the reel of it. He went to Europe. Yeah. Plenty of everything. Yeah.
He's a great guy, isn't he?
Oh, yeah. I'm going to see him someday. Yeah. I'm going to do like, bro, I'm going to take out and then I'm going to go there on the way to see who I, who'll live it.
Yeah. I wish I'd brought some pictures of Roy Palmer, but I'll send you a picture to show you the way Roy looks. He looks wonderful. He looks as good and young as ever. He really does.
Yeah, he looks almost like he does in that picture, doesn't he?

Yeah, he's hardly changed. His hair isn't gray. I'm not, I'm trying to, I don't have any hair at all. I don't have any. I don't have any. But Roy looks, his hair is still dark and he doesn't play trombone anymore, but he's still interested in it.
He had a loan in the Alva Wood six, seven years back.
Well, he gave that up on his own Wells Street, about 51, can't remember the number.
I can easily get that because I got a nephew there. He's an extra specialist at Chicago. I got two or three there, a barber.

Yeah, well, I'll send you that number anyway. All right, I appreciate that. It's down near 51st Street in Wells, across from the little school. And his wife used to play trombone too. She was very wealthy. I don't know if you knew her, but I don't think she came from here.

No, I don't remember. He had no wife up there. He had a bar woman. That sometimes works out for the best. Well, we read something, Ron, if you remember one? Oh yeah, we had the time. Green Miner. Ha ha ha ha. 239. How you call that street? Roads, eh? Yeah. Where Jesus is there. Roads have one.
That's where the Royal Garden is right on that road.
No, Royal Garden was that was in College Grove.
Oh, I thought the roads ran in there too, didn't it?
No. That's a... That's a...

the 35th Street up there. 35th Street. It's all torn down. Everything is down there. Dreamland and 35th Street may be there. Porter's Drugswood, that's down too. Upstairs, all that's down. One of the E-Lights is there. One of them is there at 35th and the State.
He liked number two. Number two. Keep enjoying that.
Mr. Bray, what kind of a style is Sugar John? You told me before that he was your first trumpet player. Nice trumpet player. What kind of a style did he play? I don't know. I couldn't tell you.
But he's a smooth trumpet player. He's a pretty honest style of bunk. Bunkway on smooth. On the order of bunk too. Yeah, smooth, smooth trumpet player. Good morning.
When was your last band about then? After the Banner band, did you give up playing dances

and just start teaching or writing? After the Banner, after the Banner we, at least, I was with the Black Eagle before I joined the band. That's the way it happened. We decided to break the Black Eagle up to reinforce the Banner band, which we did. And I took Ike Tomlin and went to New Iberic. And then the high stage they ever saw. And I came here and organized a little five-piece band right here. I had Frank Brown and Joe and Drum and Bo Frey and Clifton who was playing the banjo. He was in the French Quarter. I played plenty of banjo. Very good. I had Bill Newton on the bass. I had a pretty good five-reggie education right here. Good one. So you're writing songs now? I'm not, not no more. I wrote three. You have written songs. I wrote three and stopped, but I got two in the trunk. They're supposed to be some word added to it. I'm not ready for writing words now. I'm trying to see how those three are going to take out. Do you do any teaching now? I taught one to Professor Roger that, the Reed section right there at Professor Paul Grove School here, the Reed section. And I taught Gobert a couple of players around him, Abraham, the banjo.
Are there any good old style bands here around in this part of the country anymore? No. The trombonist Gus, I can't remember his last name. Point net.
I have his band. Oh yeah, the band. Still got the band of band here. I guess you call it something else but it. I heard them but... He still play, play the piano trombone.
Yes, he's very good. He's playing right now?
Yeah. Trombone, bartending the day for the piano.
Well, that tape is just about around the corner. Yeah, I guess. Any other questions you'd like to...
No, I was thinking if Lawrence knew Johnny Dodds. Oh, for sure. Oh yeah. Johnny is one of my favorite clarinet singers. Oh yeah?

Yeah. Well, I... Johnny Dodd took over after I left Kid Ory. That's who I used to be. Yeah. Yeah, he started with Kid Ory after. I left Kid Ory. And Jimmy Noon, I guess you knew him. Oh yeah, he... He was playing one cabaret, I was playing the other when he went up to country. Another good Tony's clarinet.

Yeah, he used to get around very fast on the clarinet. Yeah. Did the old time fellas though, like the T.O's and Warner and some of those, get all over the clarinet and the clarinet up high and low and... Oh, I don't know. Run all over the clarinet.

Oh yeah, Bach-Ate, Bach-Ate, T.O. Oh yeah, that's bad. With all the arpeggios and the chords, they didn't just stick to the melody of them. Oh, no, no, they didn't run up that scale. Somebody told me maybe they... Diminished, diminished with them. Yeah, all the different... Variations, kind of variation. Oh, it's really bad clarinet, Bach-Ate, T.O.
Did you hear Charlie McCurdy?
Oh, he is a good one too, with the rubber shorts. He was a good one too. He was a good one. Charlie McCurdy, yeah.
Who was in the Bolden band when you heard them? Can you remember? No, but their list is right there.
Yeah.
I can't remember.
I think Frank Lewis, they said, played with him for a while. I think so. Frank Lewis and... What do you call that black fella?
One, Brock.

Brock. Brock, the Brock guitar. Willa Warner. They had two clarinet, Willa Warner. They had two clarinet, Willa Warner. They had two clarinet, yeah. And Willa Warner, yeah. Jimmy Johnson on the drums. Jimmy Johnson, that's a part of one of the drums. Henry Zeno on the drums. That's that thing, that's the Bolden band.
And Batty's Delaney on trombone.
That's right. Who were some of the best trombonists you ever heard, if you can remember, aside from people

like Ory? Zoo Robson. Zoo Robson. Zoo Robson. Well done, good trombone play. I was done with Zoo Robson. How'd you like Roy? Roy Palmer, good trombone play, but Ory, you know, Ory had that stuff with him. Yeah. Ory too, good trombone play, Ory.
Well, I think, anyway, we have your birth date down and when you went to Chicago and a few of those bands straightened out now.
So, how many years have you been living here in Lafayette, Mr. Dewey?
No, I've been here, I came here, I've been here, I'm here now, 31 years, I'm not here. 31 years?
31. You're living right in the same house?
No, I came here rooming and I got tired of moving, so I bought here. Yeah, we really have a very nice house.
It's not like it's supposed to be, but I'm comfortable. Boy, it's nice. That's the main thing.
Yeah, that's enough occupation for three people, that's all it is. My life is my family, one daughter and a wife, that's all. That's all. . . .
